solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: New line backward poet pens for explorer

indicators.note: to pen something is to shut it in an enclosure, so one piece is held inside another
going backward means running from the far end, so the assembled letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
L is the abbreviation for line
W. B. Yeats, the Irish poet

explanation.surface: A poet writes a fresh line looking back on the life of a great explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: N and L go inside YEATS to make YELNATS, and only then is the whole thing turned round to give STANLEY; 'backward' looks as if it belongs to 'line' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Morton Stanley was the Victorian journalist who travelled through central Africa and famously found Livingstone.

clue.text: Comedic instrument absurd: what else is new?

indicators.note: something absurd is nonsensical and disordered, so the letters are jumbled into another arrangement

blocks.note: the thirteen letters are used exactly as printed

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs at a ridiculous novelty instrument, sighing that nothing surprises them any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What else is new?' reads as a weary catchphrase, but it supplies the thirteen letters of SWANEE WHISTLE; the punctuation is pure camouflage.
explanation.definitionFit: A slide whistle with a plunger, used for sliding cartoon-style sound effects and gags in comic music and children's shows.

clue.text: Attack in rising British submarine

indicators.note: something found in a phrase sits within its letters, spanning the gap between words
in a down clue, rising means travelling upward, so the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters at the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A British submarine surfaces to launch an attack.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters H-SUB-MA straddle 'British submarine'; read upward they spell AMBUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise assault launched from a concealed position, so the noun works as a synonym.

clue.text: Sad US city people submit

blocks.note: Los Angeles
men are people
to table a motion is to submit it for discussion

explanation.surface: A gloomy American city where the residents have simply given in.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage to table a proposal is to put it forward for debate, the opposite of the American sense of shelving it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lamentable deserves sorrow or regret, so it is a close synonym for unfortunate and deplorable.

clue.text: Swiftian lout‘s web portal

blocks.note: first meaning: the brutish human creatures in Gulliver's Travels
second meaning: the long-running internet search and news site

explanation.surface: A boorish character from Jonathan Swift turns out to run an internet homepage.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift invented the word for the savage humanoids in Gulliver's Travels, and it survives as a term for any coarse oaf.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both Swift's degraded humans, now any uncouth hooligan, and the famous internet company's homepage.

clue.text: Follow clubs playing well

blocks.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
a player on form is performing well

explanation.surface: A fan follows the football clubs that are currently playing well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' here is the card suit, not a sports team.
explanation.definitionFit: To conform is to comply with rules or obey a convention, which is following them.

clue.text: Able to take part in sport, preserving body

blocks.note: to contest an event in a game or race
the National Trust, the British organisation that conserves historic houses and landscapes

explanation.surface: An athlete fit to play sport while keeping the body in good shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preserving body' looks like looking after one's physique; it is the National Trust, a charity that preserves Britain's historic buildings, abbreviated NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Competent means having enough skill or capability to do something properly, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Genre of number one by Queen

blocks.note: NO is the abbreviation for number
the Roman numeral for one
R for Regina, the Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A music fan asks what style the band Queen's chart-topping hit belongs to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' and 'Queen' tempt a pop-chart reading, but they break into NO, I and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Noir is the crime-fiction and film style of dark, cynical stories, a recognised category of storytelling.

clue.text: Choose current film for positive thinker

blocks.note: to opt is to choose
I is the symbol for electric current
a film of mist is a thin haze

explanation.surface: Picking a recent movie suits someone with a cheerful outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current film' looks like a movie now showing; current is I from physics and film is a thin layer, MIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An optimist always expects good outcomes and looks on the bright side, so the phrase describes them.

clue.text: Poor Red Army contingent capturing one

indicators.note: to capture is to take and hold prisoner, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a red wine from Bordeaux
the Roman numeral for one
the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army

explanation.surface: A weak detachment of Soviet troops takes a single prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Army' is not the Soviet force: red is a wine, MEDOC, which captures I, and the Army contingent is RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediocre means of only ordinary or low quality, so it matches the adjective describing substandard work.

clue.text: American cartel ultimately behind recording

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for American
the closing letter of the word
British slang for the backside

explanation.surface: A US drug cartel is secretly financing a record release.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like a preposition but is the noun for one's rear, which British slang calls a bum.
explanation.definitionFit: An album is a collection of tracks issued together as a single record or release.

clue.text: Awkward amateur is retained by FT news boss

indicators.note: something retained by another is kept inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a ham is an amateur, as in ham radio
taken as written
taken as written
ED is short for editor, who runs a newspaper

explanation.surface: A clumsy beginner has been kept on by the Financial Times editor.
explanation.walkthrough: FT, the Financial Times, really is the paper here, but only as two letters holding IS; 'news boss' is a separate ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham-fisted means clumsy with the hands or tactless in handling something, a synonym for awkward.

clue.text: Leader once from Eire – he’s now abroad

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or all over the place, so the letters are scattered into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the ten letters used as printed

explanation.surface: A former Irish leader who has since emigrated.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to an Irish politician living overseas; the letters of 'Eire he's now' rearrange into the American president.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwight Eisenhower was the Second World War Allied commander and later United States president, so a past head of state.

clue.text: This is to be loaded, having boundless wealth

indicators.note: without bounds means without its limits, so the first and last letters are cut off

blocks.note: Mammon is wealth personified as a false god

explanation.surface: Being loaded means having boundless riches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaded' suggests rich, which the surface reinforces, but the definition means put into a gun; Mammon loses its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammunition, informally shortened, is what a gun or weapon is charged with before firing.

clue.text: Understood old men on board lose control

blocks.note: to get something is to understand it
O is the abbreviation for old
chess men are pieces

explanation.surface: Veteran sailors realise they are no longer in charge of the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a ship's crew, but the board is a chessboard and its men are the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pieces is an idiom for breaking down emotionally and failing to cope under pressure.

clue.text: Agitator departs escaping volatile Belarus border

indicators.note: something escaping gets away and leaves, so a letter is removed from the rest
volatile means unstable and liable to change, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
the letters used as printed

explanation.surface: A troublemaker slips out of the tense frontier region of Belarus.
explanation.walkthrough: Take D out of 'Belarus border' and rearrange the twelve letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabble-rouser stirs up crowds to anger or unrest, which is what an agitator does.

clue.text: Second question in old magazine

blocks.note: to second a proposal is to support or back it
an issue is a question under debate

explanation.surface: A follow-up quiz question printed in an old periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like a number or a moment of time; it is the verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: A back issue is an earlier edition of a periodical, no longer the current one on sale.

clue.text: What about a fling where travellers go?

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: eh? is a request to repeat, like what?
taken as written
to fling is to throw

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a holiday romance at a resort where tourists head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What about a fling' reads as a proposal of romance; fling is a throw, and Heathrow is London's main airport.
explanation.definitionFit: Heathrow is London's largest airport, a place passengers pass through on journeys abroad.

clue.text: Force to serve port in China

blocks.note: first meaning: to kidnap someone into working as a sailor
second meaning: the great city on the Yangtze delta

explanation.surface: Conscripted to work at a Chinese harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb came from the practice of drugging men and sending them on ships bound for the Far East.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to press-gang or coerce someone into labour, and the noun names China's biggest seaport city.

clue.text: What draws vampire close to victim?

definitions.text: What draws vampire close to victim?

blocks.clueFragment: What draws vampire close to victim?
blocks.note: surface reading: the lure that tempts Dracula towards his prey
setter's reading: a vampire bat, which finds its prey by sound reflected off it

explanation.walkthrough: The vampire is not the horror-film count but the bat, which navigates in the dark by emitting calls and hearing them bounce back.
explanation.definitionFit: Bats send out high-pitched sounds and judge distance from the returning reflections, a sense that guides them onto prey.

clue.text: Water level rising over king in cutter?

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means travelling upward, so the letters run from bottom to top

blocks.note: the tide is the rising and falling level of the sea
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
R for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Flood waters climb above a monarch aboard a small boat.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is a boat, but the question mark warns of a punning definition: an editor cuts text and film.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor trims and shortens copy or footage, so whimsically they are a person who cuts things.

clue.text: Severe test of French in viva voce

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: de is French for of
a viva voce is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A gruelling French examination conducted out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Viva voce is Latin for 'with the living voice'; universities use it for a spoken exam, also called an oral.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful or harrowing experience that tests endurance, as was the medieval trial by ordeal.

clue.text: Hair colouring can end in disappointment

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: a tin is a can
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Dyeing your hair can leave you let down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb meaning may; it is a noun, the container TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A tint is a semi-permanent dye applied to give hair a different shade.

clue.text: Gallup employee’s camera accessory?

blocks.note: setter's reading: a pollster's job is to discover people's opinions
surface reading: the eyepiece a photographer looks through

explanation.walkthrough: Gallup is the US opinion-polling firm; a worker there seeks out people's views, so is literally a view finder.
explanation.definitionFit: The camera's framing window shows what the lens sees, and a pollster, punningly, discovers opinions.

clue.text: Opportunity to forget name woman left

indicators.note: something forgotten is left out entirely, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: a window of opportunity
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A chance to forget the name of a woman who walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' suggests departure, but here a woman left behind after her husband died.
explanation.definitionFit: A widow is a woman whose husband has died, so she has been left alone, a cryptic paraphrase.

clue.text: Carbon works in Barrow

blocks.note: the chemical symbol for carbon
works of art

explanation.surface: A carbon plant operating in the town of Barrow.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrow-in-Furness is a shipbuilding town in Cumbria, England, but here barrow is the small handcart.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow is a small hand-pushed vehicle for carrying loads, a kind of cart.

clue.text: Went through red here as tipsy

indicators.note: someone tipsy is unsteady and staggering, so the letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: the nine letters used as printed

explanation.surface: A tipsy driver ran a red light at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went through red' paints a driver jumping a traffic light, but the definition is just the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To go through a speech or play is to practise it from start to finish, which is rehearsing.

clue.text: Attractive person caught you texting link

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
U is text-message shorthand for you
a tie is a link or bond

explanation.surface: A good-looking person spotted you sending a link by message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like spotted, but it is the cricket abbreviation C.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutie is informal for someone who is charming and good-looking.

clue.text: See 1 down
Profligate succeeded in temple on lake

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in genealogies
a wat is a Buddhist temple in Thailand or Cambodia
re means on or concerning
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A spendthrift prospered inside a lakeside shrine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a positional word; it is RE, meaning about, a common crossword equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: A profligate squanders money recklessly, and a wastrel is a good-for-nothing spendthrift.
